topics.title: Types & Variables
topics.subtitle: Naming and categorising data
teaching: A variable is a named slot that holds a value. You give it a name so you can refer to that value later — instead of writing the number 42 everywhere, you write age.

Every value has a type — the kind of data it is. Common types: integer (whole number), float (decimal number), string (text), bool (true/false). Types matter because they control what operations are valid and how much memory is used.

In dynamically typed languages like Python the type is attached to the value, not the variable — you can reassign a variable to a completely different type. In statically typed languages like C, Rust, and UniLogic the type is fixed at compile time and violations are caught before the program runs.

code_blocks.code:
age = 25          # int
name = "Alice"    # str
price = 9.99      # float
active = True     # bool

print(type(age))  # <class 'int'>

var age   : Int  = 25
var name  : Str  = "Alice"
var price : F64  = 9.99
var active: Bool = true

exercises.question: Which type would you use to store the number of students in a class (e.g. 30)?
options: bool — it's either zero or not
exercises.explanation: A student count is always a whole number, so an integer is the right choice. Floats carry unnecessary overhead for values that are never fractional.

exercises.question: What keyword does Python use to declare a variable? (just type the keyword, lowercase)
exercises.explanation: Python has no keyword — you declare a variable just by assigning to it: x = 5. The variable springs into existence on first assignment.

topics.title: Functions
topics.subtitle: Reusable code blocks with inputs and outputs
teaching: A function is a named block of code that does one thing. You define it once and call it as many times as you need — write the logic once, reuse it everywhere.
Functions take parameters (inputs) and return a value (output). Good functions are small, focused, and named clearly after what they do: add_tax, is_valid_email, send_message.
Functions also create a scope — variables declared inside a function are invisible outside it. This prevents code in different parts of a program from accidentally interfering with each other.

code_blocks.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(3, 4)   # result = 7
print(result)

exercises.question: What is the term for the values you pass into a function when calling it?
exercises.explanation: The values passed at call-time are called arguments. The names in the function definition are parameters. In casual use both words are common.

exercises.question: In Python, what keyword starts a function definition?
exercises.explanation: def is Python's keyword for defining a function: def my_function():

topics.title: If / Else Logic
topics.subtitle: Making decisions based on conditions
teaching: Programs need to make decisions. If/else lets a program run different code depending on whether a condition is true or false.
A condition is any expression that evaluates to a boolean — true or false. Comparison operators: == (equal), != (not equal), < > <= >=. Logical operators: and / &&, or / ||, not / !.
You can chain conditions with else if (called elif in Python) to test multiple possibilities in sequence. Only the first matching branch runs.

exercises.question: Which operator checks if two values are equal (not assigning, but comparing)?
exercises.explanation: == compares two values for equality. = is assignment (sets a variable). Mixing them up is one of the most common bugs in programming.

exercises.question: In Python, what is the keyword for 'else if'? (type it exactly)
exercises.explanation: Python uses elif as a contraction of else if. Most other languages spell it out as else if.

topics.title: Loops
topics.subtitle: Repeating code efficiently
teaching: A loop repeats a block of code. Without loops you'd have to write the same line hundreds of times. There are two main kinds: for loops (repeat a known number of times or over a collection) and while loops (repeat as long as a condition is true).

The for loop is used when you know the range ahead of time, or when you want to process every item in a list. The while loop is used when you don't know how many iterations you need — you keep going until a condition becomes false.
Two control keywords: break exits the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next.

code_blocks.code:
# for loop — count 0 to 4
for i in range(5):
    print(i)   # prints 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

# while loop
count = 0
while count < 3:
    print(count)
    count += 1   # prints 0, 1, 2

exercises.question: Which loop type is best when you don't know in advance how many iterations are needed?
options: for loop — it always knows the count
while loop — it runs until a condition becomes false
exercises.explanation: A while loop keeps running as long as its condition is true, making it ideal when the iteration count is unknown — e.g. reading input until the user types 'quit'.

exercises.question: What keyword immediately exits a loop (stops it completely)?
exercises.explanation: break exits the nearest enclosing loop. continue skips to the next iteration instead.

topics.title: Collections
topics.subtitle: Storing and iterating over multiple values
teaching: Instead of having a separate variable for each value, collections let you group many values under one name. The most common are arrays (fixed-size, same type) and lists (dynamic size).
You access items by index — a position number starting at 0. Index 0 is the first item, index 1 is the second, and so on. Accessing an index that doesn't exist causes an error (index out of bounds).

Other common collection types: dictionary / map — key/value pairs (like a phone book). set — unique values only, no duplicates. Each has different performance characteristics depending on the operation.

code_blocks.code:
# List — dynamic, any type
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[0])   # apple

fruits.append("date")   # add item

# Dictionary
ages = {"Alice": 30, "Bob": 25}
print(ages["Alice"])   # 30

# Loop over a list
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

exercises.question: If a list has 5 items, what is the index of the last item?
exercises.explanation: Indices start at 0. A list of 5 items has indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The last item is always at index length - 1, which is 4 here.

exercises.question: What index accesses the FIRST element of any list or array?
exercises.explanation: All mainstream languages (Python, C, Rust, UniLogic, Java, JavaScript…) use 0-based indexing. The first element is always at index 0.

topics.title: Objects & Inheritance
topics.subtitle: Bundling data and behaviour
teaching: A class is a blueprint for creating objects. It bundles related data (called fields or attributes) and behaviour (called methods) into one unit. An object is one instance of a class — created from the blueprint.

Inheritance lets one class extend another. The child class gets all the fields and methods of the parent, and can add or override them. This avoids duplicating code when two things are similar but not identical.

C doesn't have classes — it uses struct for grouping data, and function pointers for behaviour. Rust uses struct with impl blocks and traits instead of inheritance. Python and UniLogic have full class-based inheritance.

exercises.question: What is an 'object' in object-oriented programming?
options: One specific instance created from a class
A function that belongs to a module
exercises.explanation: A class is the blueprint; an object is a specific instance built from that blueprint. You can create many objects from one class, each with their own data.

exercises.question: What is the term for when a child class provides its own version of a method defined in the parent class?
exercises.explanation: Overriding (or method overriding) is when a subclass replaces a method inherited from its parent. The child's version runs instead of the parent's.

topics.title: Language Deep Dive
topics.subtitle: What makes each language distinctive
teaching: Python — beginner-friendly, dynamically typed, garbage-collected. Ideal for scripting, data science, and rapid prototyping. Slower than compiled languages but readable and concise. Huge standard library.

C — the foundation of modern computing. No garbage collector, no runtime overhead. You manage memory manually with malloc/free. Fast, low-level, but unforgiving — undefined behaviour and memory bugs are real risks. Used in OS kernels, embedded systems, and anywhere performance is critical.

Rust — systems-level performance like C, but with a compiler that eliminates memory bugs at compile time through its ownership model. No garbage collector, no null pointer exceptions, no data races. Steeper learning curve, but the compiler catches entire classes of bugs before the program runs.

UniLogic — compiles to multiple targets (native binary, bytecode, WASM). Statically typed, clean syntax. Designed for code that needs to run on different platforms without rewriting. The language this IDE is built for.

code_blocks.code:
# Python: concise, no types needed
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

print(greet("World"))   # Hello, World!

exercises.question: Which language uses an 'ownership model' to prevent memory bugs at compile time, with no garbage collector?
options: Rust — the borrow checker enforces ownership rules
exercises.explanation: Rust's borrow checker is a compile-time analysis that enforces ownership rules — ensuring no two parts of the program can mutate the same data simultaneously, and all allocations are freed exactly once.

exercises.question: What is the name of the memory management technique Python uses (hint: it counts how many references point to each object)?
exercises.explanation: Python uses reference counting — each object tracks how many variables point to it. When that count reaches zero, the object is freed. A cycle-detector handles circular references.
